content: Dover's powder was a historical medicinal preparation used to treat symptoms of colds and fevers. It is no longer utilized in modern medical practice. The powder was named after Dr. Thomas Dover, an 18th-century English physician who first formulated it. The composition of Dover's powder included powdered ipecacuanha (a substance now used to produce syrup of ipecac), powdered opium, and sulphate of potash. This preparation was commonly employed in domestic medicine to induce sweating (diaphoresis), which was believed to help counteract the progression of a cold or to address the early stages of a fever. It was also referred to by its Latin name, pulvis ipecacuanhae et opii. For optimal effectiveness as a sudorific, it was advised that the patient consume large quantities of a warm, non-irritating beverage after taking the powder. An example of its use is documented in a report by Dr. Sharp, a physician serving in the British naval forces stationed in the West Indies, specifically in Trinidad, in 1818. Dr. Sharp described its application in the treatment of acute dysentery cases. He noted that among thirty cases of dysentery, including nineteen individuals who had recently arrived from Europe, the symptoms were generally mild. The disease responded well to standard treatments of the time, which included bloodletting when vascular conditions warranted it, as well as the administration of small, repeated doses of saline purgatives. Additionally, small doses of calomel (mercurous chloride) and opium were given at bedtime, along with infusions of ipecacuanha or Dover's powder. These treatments, combined with the use of tonics, moderate consumption of port wine, and a light diet based on starchy foods, typically resulted in a complete recovery.
